title: Next Questions
text:
Reading guide (1 min)

In this cycle, the priority is not to add more questions, but to recompute the four axes below under the same definitions.
Directional judgment should rely on whether the same metric moves in the same direction across at least two recalculations, not on a single observed value.

title: Next Questions
text:
Recurring questions for this cycle (4)

Q1. Is policy-source concentration easing, stable, or intensifying?

Observation baseline: The report frames hub-channel concentration as a headline message; for repeated monitoring, this becomes a practical baseline for policy-source-country concentration.
Current baseline: The combined share of the top three policy-source countries is 50.6%. At the same time, volume hubs and density hubs diverge, and domain composition changes by source type (Interactive Figures 5-7).
Checks: Top-3 policy-source-country share, changes in the ordering of leading source countries, overlap between top-volume and top-density groups, and directional shifts in source-type-by-domain composition.
Completion signal: After at least two recalculations under the same definition, the direction can be classified as easing, stable, or intensifying.
See also: Interactive Figure 5 · Interactive Figure 6 · Interactive Figure 7 · Appendix C9



Q2. Is the share of repeatedly cited papers expanding or shrinking?

Observation baseline: The report sets 48.1% as the starting baseline for the share of papers cited by at least two different policy documents.
Current baseline: Among 6,532,365 unique cited papers, 48.1% are cited repeatedly by two or more distinct policy documents.
Checks: Sensitivity across >=2 / >=5 / >=10 thresholds, repeated citation by publication-year cohort, and changes in the long-tail distribution (CCDF).
Completion signal: The same directional change appears across threshold and cohort checks, while separating recent-paper disadvantage from structural change.
See also: Appendix: repeated-citation share definition · Appendix C6 · Appendix C10



Q3. Is the research cited by Korean policy documents becoming more diversified?

Observation baseline: The report summarizes that research cited by Korean policy documents is concentrated in U.S.-authored research at 55.7% among citations with known first-author country codes.
Current baseline: U.S.-authored research accounts for 55.7%, while Korean-authored research accounts for 4.5% (7.7 times the expected share of 0.6%).
Checks: Top-1 country share, combined top-3 country share, domain-level composition of cited research, stability of the domestic-citation share, and sensitivity to author-country rules.
Completion signal: Top-country concentration and domestic/non-domestic composition can be explained in the same direction, and the interpretation remains stable under alternative author-country rules.
See also: Interactive Figure 9 · Interactive Figure 10 · Interactive Figure 11 · Appendix C12



Q4. Are the policy-entry routes for Korean research becoming broader?

Observation baseline: The report states that policy citations to Korean research are concentrated in the top three policy-source tags: United States, international organizations, and United Kingdom.
Current baseline: Under policy-source tags, the United States accounts for 27.8%, international organizations for 19.4%, and the United Kingdom for 7.7%, giving a combined top-3 share of 54.8%.
Checks: Combined top-3 policy-source share, changes in source ordering, domain-level composition of policy citations to Korean research, and stability after deduplication.
Completion signal: The trend in top-source concentration can be recalculated stably under the same deduplication rule, and route broadening can be explained as a change in route structure rather than a single rank shift.
See also: Interactive Figure 11 · Interactive Figure 12 · Appendix C8 · Appendix C13

Where the larger movements occur

1. Korea’s two directional routes

The top-3 share for inbound policy citations to Korean research falls from 54.8% -> 51.1%.

This does not require rewriting the report’s core sentence, but the Korea section should be read as showing somewhat weaker concentration in the updated data. See the Appendix and Interactive pages for the surrounding diagnostics.


2. Domestic-citation share

Korea’s domestic-citation share falls from 4.5% -> 3.8%.
The expected domestic-citation share rises from 0.59% -> 0.72%.

This Supplementary Information (SI) page is the companion layer to the Main Report (Korean PDF). While the PDF keeps the public-facing narrative short, this web layer keeps background notes, method checks, diagnostics, and interactive exploration in one place.

title: Supplementary Information — Overview
text:
Background notes

Why read hubs as routes, not as rankings?
The hub section is not a simple ranking of “top” policy channels. Even among leading sources, the channels with the largest total citation volume can differ from the channels that cite research most densely, and domain portfolios also change by source type.
The more useful question is therefore not “who is first?” but “which channels repeatedly bring research into policy documents?”


Why separate Korea’s inbound and policy-sourcing routes?
The key Korean message is not that 54.8% and 55.7% look similar. It is that one is a top-3 channel concentration and the other is a top-1 country concentration.
If inbound routes and policy-sourcing routes are collapsed into a single score, that structural difference disappears.


Why are “two speeds” a practical question?
Policy evidence does not move at one speed. Mature agendas and high-growth agendas need different update rhythms.
This is why the report separates the two-speed pattern: not to create another topic ranking, but to show that evidence management cadence should differ by agenda type.


What changes once domestic references are linked?
To broaden the Korean reading, the international-hub view needs to be complemented with domestic policy references. Kim et al. (2025) gives an exploratory example with NKIS policy research reports, suggesting that domestic and international evidence-sourcing routes may differ by field.
This extension changes the question from “How does Korea look globally?” to “Which Korean policy actors draw on what kinds of evidence, and through which routes?”

title: Methods & Data Validity

First checks (1 min)

Before country comparison, confirm results use only citations with known first-author country codes.
Do not compare indicators with different denominators directly.
If interpretation is unclear, review Sections 1-5 in order.

title: Methods & Data Validity
text:
1) Analysis scope
Start by making the scope of the analysis explicit.

Snapshot versions: Overton 2025.02 and OpenAlex 2025.06
Unit of analysis: unique policy documents (deduplicated at the policy-document level)
Citation scope: DOI-identified scholarly citations extracted from policy references







Note



Interpretation boundary

Results are not a full census of all policy documents. They are observations within the current snapshot and matching scope.
Non-DOI evidence (reports, legal texts, web sources) is outside the default indicator set.

title: Methods & Data Validity
text:
2) Matching & missingness checks

The DOI → OpenAlex matching rate and country-code missingness are primary safety checks.
For country comparisons, first confirm the denominator uses citations with known first-author country codes.

Details: - Appendix B0-1. Matching & missingness - Appendix B0. Quick definitions

title: Methods & Data Validity
text:
3) Core metric definitions (summary)
The definitions below provide a minimum baseline for re-reading the headline numbers.

Citation counts vs unique works: separate frequency from breadth
Recency: share of policy citations to works published in 2022-2024
Citation intensity: citation counts / unique works within an aggregation unit
Domestic-citation share: country-level same-country citation share, computed only over citations with known first-author country codes

Details: - Citations vs works - Recency / intensity - Domestic-citation share

title: Methods & Data Validity
text:
4) Interpretation guardrails
The items below are the minimum checks needed before reading the results too strongly.

Multi-label topics can produce totals above 100%.
Recent-year declines may reflect observation/accumulation lag rather than a structural reversal.
The 2012 mean spike should be read with distribution diagnostics (median/trimmed mean), not a single average.

Details: - Multi-label topics - Recent-year decline caution - Why 2012 looks high

title: Methods & Data Validity
text:
5) Recompute/update protocol
Finally, the same checks should be repeatable in the next update cycle.

Recompute the same indicators quarterly or biannually and track directional state (rising/stable/easing).
Keep the main report headline-focused, while updating formulas, sensitivity checks, and supporting tables in the SI layer.
Record all figure/text changes and rebuilt outputs in the update log.

title: Appendix
text:
A. Coverage & tagging
This section provides the minimum context needed before reading the hub results. The observable policy-document universe in Overton may be uneven across countries and source types, so tagging rules and coverage gaps should be checked first.

A1. Policy document coverage map (documents by policy source country)






Note



Display rules (summary)

Use top-level country tags only (exclude sub-tags like USA > California)
Exclude IGO / EU
Use a log scale for coloring due to large cross-country variance




  
    Open in new tab
    May load slowly
    Load plot
  



A2. Why exclude sub-tags (A > B) and keep top-level country tags only
Overton policy source country tags include country-level tags (e.g., USA, UK) and sub-regional tags (e.g., USA > California). To align meaning with OpenAlex country codes, this report uses top-level country tags only for default aggregations.
This simplifies country-level comparisons. At the same time, it can invite under/over-interpretation when sub-tags contribute heavily. So, when reading country comparisons, it is safer to check coverage itself as well.


A3. Why do we need exceptions for Hong Kong / Georgia
Policy source country tags can appear only as sub-tags such as China > Hong Kong and USA > Georgia. If we keep only top-level tags, these can be filtered out from the policy-source side. That can make them look like “policy sources that do not exist” in the network view. For network figures, we therefore split China > Hong Kong into Hong Kong and USA > Georgia into Georgia (USA).


More detail: sub-tag scale, examples, and Hong Kong notation


Data snapshot: Overton 2025.02
The numbers below are summaries computed from the Overton 2025.02 snapshot.

By policy document counts: sub-tags total 200,381 out of 1,671,835 (12.0%)
By DOI citation records: sub-tags total 3,488,024 out of 48,456,680 (7.2%)

Here, “DOI citation records” are raw-record totals, and may differ from analysis-ready deduplicated counts shown in the main report key-number block.
Top-level parents with large sub-tag contributions are typically USA, Spain, Canada, Australia, UK (in that order).


Top sub-tag examples (by policy document counts)

Is Hong Kong “merged into China” here?
In the current snapshot, Overton policy sources do not include Hong Kong as a top-level country tag. It is observed only as China > Hong Kong (1,182 policy documents). By contrast, OpenAlex research countries use a separate code HK → Hong Kong.
If we aggregate policy sources using top-level tags only, documents under China > Hong Kong drop from the policy-source side. Meanwhile, Hong Kong remains only as a research-country node. This can make it look like a “cited-only node.”


Caution: naive sub-tag replacement causes collisions
If you naively map A > B → B, then USA > Georgia (the US state) collides with Georgia (the country). If you want to re-attribute sub-tags at country scale, it is safer to separate two steps: (1) lifting to parent (A > B → A) and (2) exception handling (whether to treat Hong Kong as its own unit).

title: Appendix
text:
B. Definitions & interpretation
This section brings together the denominator, definition, and interpretation notes needed to re-read the main-report metrics safely. The same number can imply different conclusions when denominators differ, so these conditions should be checked first.

B0. Quick definitions (summary)

Unit of analysis: Overton policy documents are deduplicated at the policy-document level and treated as “unique policy documents.” See: DOI-citation coverage share
Citation counts vs unique works: “how often” vs “how widely” are different questions, so we separate them. See: Citations vs works
Recency / intensity: recency is the share of policy citations to works published in 2022-2024; intensity is average policy citations per unique work. See: Recency / intensity
Multi-label topics: OpenAlex topics are multi-label; a single work can belong to multiple topics, so shares can exceed 100%. See: Multi-label

B1. DOI-citation coverage share (97.6%): denominator
What denominator does “97.6%” use in this snapshot?
We deduplicated Overton policy documents at the policy-document level to build 1,381,084 unique policy documents. Then we counted whether each document contains at least one DOI-based scholarly citation. As a result, 1,347,563 documents (97.6%) contain at least one DOI citation.






Note



Interpretation boundary

This is not the share of “all policy documents” that cite science. It is the share within the set of policy documents collected in the Overton snapshot.

What does “deduplication” mean here?
Raw Overton policy documents can include duplicates (versions, re-posts, language variants, metadata duplication). For analysis, we unify them at the policy-document level to treat them as unique policy documents.

B2. Repeat-citation share (48.1%): definition
What does “48.1% are repeatedly cited (>=2)” mean in this analysis snapshot?
This metric summarizes, among unique cited works, how many are called repeatedly across different policy documents.

Unit: unique cited works (OpenAlex works)
Computation: after cleaning policy→work DOI links, count how many distinct policy documents (unique documents) cite each work
Definition: “repeatedly cited (>=2)” means cited by at least two distinct policy documents

In the Overton 2025.02×OpenAlex 2025.06 linked data, 3,143,234 out of 6,532,365 unique cited works (48.1%) are cited by two or more policy documents.






Note



Interpretation boundary

As with the 97.6% statistic, this number is limited to the DOI-linked observed scope in the snapshot.
Citations without DOIs (reports, legislation, web sources, etc.) are not included in this repeated-call calculation.





B3. Citations vs works
Why separate “citation counts” and “unique works”?

Citation counts: total number of DOI citation records (how many times policy documents cite DOI works)
Unique works: the number of distinct cited works after deduplicating citations by work identity

The questions “how often does policy cite evidence?” (frequency) and “how wide is the evidence pool?” (diversity) are different, so we interpret them separately.


B4. Recency / intensity
How are “recency” and “citation intensity” computed?

Recency: the share of policy citations to works published in 2022-2024
Citation intensity: average policy citations per unique work in the aggregation unit = citations / unique works



B5. Domestic-citation share
How is domestic-citation share computed?
We map policy source country tags to 2-letter country codes (e.g., USA → US, UK → GB), and compute country-level domestic-citation share using only citations with known first-author country codes as the denominator. That is, domestic-citation share is not a pattern over “all citations.” It is a pattern over citations where the first-author country code is available. The older internal label could be misleading; in this English SI, “domestic-citation share” is used to avoid confusion with author- or article-level citation behavior.


More: expected-share definition and a comparison table

How is expected domestic-citation share computed?
For each policy source country, we first compute its domain mix of cited research. For each domain, we multiply by the country’s global research production share in that domain (OpenAlex), then sum across domains. Conceptually:
expected = sum( policy_citation_domain_share * global_production_share_in_domain )

Why define policy-source → research-country flows by first-author country?
First-author affiliation country is the most consistently extractable country attribute. However, it does not reflect coauthor distributions, corresponding authors, or multi-affiliation cases, so it must be interpreted as an “approximation with limited representativeness.”



B6. Multi-label topics
Why can topic/domain shares exceed 100%?
OpenAlex topics are multi-label. A single work can belong to multiple topics simultaneously, so aggregations by topic/domain/subfield can double-count. Topic-based numbers should be read as “topic-instance based.”
In the topic data used here, a single policy citation is linked to about 2.8 topics on average. Therefore, summing by domain/topic yields totals larger than raw citation counts.
However, if we fractionally allocate each citation across the work’s topic count, the domain ranking is preserved and the top-3 domain share changes only slightly (e.g., 88.8% → 88.5%).
Can source-country / source-type totals also grow beyond 100%?
Yes. Overton source country/type labels are tag-based (including parent/child tags), so a single document can be counted in multiple categories.


B7. Recent-year decline caution
Does the post-2022 decline in the time trend mean “policy cites science less”?
A direct conclusion is difficult here. Coverage delays (collection/processing lags) and the fact that citations accumulate after publication likely act together. It is safer to read recent years as signals mixed with observation lag, rather than as real-time decreases.


B8. Why 2012 looks high
Why does “citations per policy document” look especially high around 2012?
When the distribution has a long tail, averages are strongly affected. When the average looks high, it is safer to first separate whether it is driven by a few extreme documents or whether the whole distribution shifted rightward.
Trimmed means exclude extreme values and help diagnose whether the average is being pulled by outliers.
The figure below shows, by year, the mean along with the median and trimmed mean. It also reports the share of citations contributed by the top 1% of documents.

Key messages:

The rise around 2012 appears not only in the mean but also in the median and trimmed mean. This suggests a mixture of distribution-wide change, not only a handful of extreme documents.
The top-1% contribution does not spike uniquely in 2012. Therefore, it is hard to attribute the 2012 peak to only a very small number of documents.



B9. OA interpretation
Is higher OA (open access) share in policy citations causal?
Observationally, OA share tends to be higher in policy-cited works. But this does not immediately imply causality (“OA causes more policy citation”). Confounders include the likelihood that policy-relevant work is published OA, public funding structure, and domain composition.
However, even when we split by domain and publication-year windows among policy-cited works, the pattern that OA works have higher average policy citations per paper largely remains.
